item.text: {"text":"Krichene and Rendle’s [On Sampled Metrics for Item Recommendation (KDD 2020)](https://research.google/pubs/on-sampled-metrics-for-item-recommendation/) is the key reference: sampled ranking metrics can reverse model comparisons even in expectation; smaller samples also make different metrics increasingly resemble AUC. Their [IJCAI extended abstract, §3.2](https://ijcai.org/proceedings/2021/651), analyzes sampled-rank distributions. For uniform sampling without replacement, the corresponding exact derivation is: with N eligible negatives, a positive at full-catalog rank r, and m sampled negatives, X ~ Hypergeometric(N, r−1, m), sampled rank = 1+X, and E[HR@K | r] = P(X ≤ K−1). Thus E[sampled rank | r] = 1+m(r−1)/N. Sampling with replacement instead gives a binomial distribution.\n\nA direct consequence for fixed scores and consistent tie-breaking: enlarging nested candidate sets cannot improve the positive’s rank, so HR@K is nonincreasing for every user. Uniform random nesting therefore also yields nonincreasing expected HR@K as candidate depth grows; independently redrawn sets can fluctuate empirically. A decline from 99 negatives toward full-catalog evaluation is consequently expected from added competition and, by itself, does not establish a newly discovered model weakness. Keep the benchmark’s candidate protocol fixed for selection; interpret depth diagnostics against this mathematical baseline. The decline’s magnitude depends on the model’s full-catalog rank distribution, so monotonicity alone supplies no universal expected degradation rate."}
